The Planned Development Districts include both Planned Residential Development (PRD) and Planned Mixed Use Development (PMXD). Developers may propose projects under the Planned Development District guidelines on properties of at least five acres. A variety of residential housing types are permitted from one story through multi-family, multi-story dwellings. Limited commercial space is permitted as well, provided the underlying zoning is not C-1 or C-2. Planned Development Districts are approved with a specific Development Plan and future development of those areas must abide by the original approved plan.
The Conservation District is located at the corner of Connor Road and Terrace Drive.

The C-2 Commercial District is composed of highway commercial developments. Buildings have larger setbacks from the roadway with dedicated on-site parking areas. Residential dwellings are also permitted, including single-family attached (rowhouses and townhomes), multi-family dwellings, and mixed-use buildings with residential above commercial. The C-2 District has the largest availability of permitted land uses, and any uses not specifically provided for elsewhere in the Zoning Ordinance may apply for a conditional use permit.

The core of the district includes restaurants, retail sales and service, medical facilities, and municipal offices. Two municipal parking garages support the needs of the district and the adjacent Mt. Lebanon PRT station, providing light rail connectivity to Downtown Pittsburgh.

On-street parking is available and supported by additional surface parking adjacent to these areas. They are designed to be walkable and provide for uses that are compatible in intensity and scale to neighboring residential areas. Restaurants and bars may not operate after 11 PM in C-1 areas.

Cemeteries are a conditional use in the district, which contains two existing cemeteries.

The R-1 Zoning District is primarily single-family residential homes with large estate-sized lots. The district is characterized by deeper front yard setbacks and tree-lined streets giving a stately neighborhood atmosphere. R-1 neighborhoods tend to have been developed as automobile-centric with long streets that wind around the topography. Conditional Uses include schools, places of worship, or public and semi-public uses such as the Library. Some R-1 properties are also part of a Continuing Care Overlay.
